en.sup: Supplied in English. The Greek participle, 'falling (to one)', leaves the person understood.

01.r: Continues the parable from its opening.

02.r: The younger son makes his request.

03.r: Picks out one of the two sons.

04.r: The younger of the two brothers.
04.n: The comparative of νέος, 'young'. Abbott-Smith notes that the Septuagint uses the comparative for Hebrew words for small or young. The BSB adds 'son'.

06.r: Marks the father of the story.
06.n: The Greek has the article, 'the father'; most translations read 'his father'. Only the YLT keeps 'the'.

09.n: An aorist imperative: a direct command, with no softening.

11.r: Goes with 'that falls': the particular share that is his.

12.r: The part of the estate that would come to him.
12.n: A present participle of a verb that means 'to cast upon' when it has an object; used without one, as here, it means to fall to someone, to belong to him. Abbott-Smith's entry as shown in our brief gives only the first sense.

13.r: His part of the family property.
13.n: Abbott-Smith: 'a part, share, portion'. This study renders μέρος 'share' and keeps 'portion' for μερίς.

14.r: The property as a known whole.

15.n: Abbott-Smith: 'substance, property', listing this verse and the next as its only New Testament uses. He derives it from οὖσα, the feminine participle of 'to be': what one has.

16.n: The article used as a pronoun, 'he'. See the note on the text.

18.n: Abbott-Smith gives 'to divide into parts' and 'to distribute', listing this verse under the second. He notes that the Septuagint uses it for Hebrew חלק, to divide.

20.n: Literally 'the living'; Greek uses the article where English uses 'his'. The YLT keeps 'the'.

21.r: What the father lived on: his means.
21.n: The word means life itself, the course of life. Abbott-Smith's second sense is 'living, livelihood, means', listing this verse. It is a different word from οὐσία, 'property', earlier in the verse; the BSB renders this one 'property'.

tr_note: The Textus Receptus reads καί, 'and', where our text has ὁ δέ, 'and he': so 'and he divided', with the subject left in the verb. The KJV's 'And he divided' reads the same either way.
